input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

input.section_title: Limitations, failure modes, and practical mitigations
input.section_summary: Discuss limitations such as small dataset scale, domain-transfer risks, and dependence on retrieval quality; enumerate practical mitigations (data augmentation, retrieval re-ranking, human-in-the-loop checks) and short-term validation strategies to detect and reduce unsupported assertions.

output:
The system described in this paper is designed with conservative evidence requirements and machine-checkable outputs, but several practical limitations and failure modes remain. Because no external retrieval excerpts are provided to substantiate empirical claims in this section, the observations and recommended mitigations below are stated as general background knowledge and practical guidance rather than validated experimental findings.

Limitations and failure modes
- Dataset scale and representativeness. The present workflow was developed and evaluated using a small, curated set of internal notes and PDFs. Small or narrowly sampled corpora limit our ability to characterize performance across domains and increase the risk that generation and retrieval components overfit to idiosyncratic phrasing or citation patterns. (General background knowledge.)
- Dependence on retrieval quality. The approach relies on retrieved evidence to ground assertions. Inadequate recall, poor ranking, or source-mismatch in the retrieval index can produce gaps that downstream generation fills with unsupported content. (General background knowledge.)
- Graph mis-specification and brittle dependency encoding. Incorrect or incomplete section dependency edges can lead to suboptimal scheduling (for example, generating a background section after dependent methods text), reducing coherence and making it harder to place citations where they are most relevant. (General background knowledge.)
- JSON-constraint tradeoffs. Enforcing strict JSON schemas improves auditability but can increase generation failure rates (invalid JSON, missing required fields) or encourage token-level strategies that meet schema constraints while evading deeper content checks (e.g., including a citation field without actually grounding assertions). (General background knowledge.)
- Assembly and bibliography consistency errors. Combining per-section JSON outputs into a LaTeX manuscript and a refs.bib may expose mismatches (duplicate keys, missing bib entries referenced in-text) and integration bugs in the assembly pipeline. (General background knowledge.)
- Human factors and workflow friction. Requiring mandatory citations and post-hoc audits increases human review burden; without careful UI and tooling, annotators or authors may find the process slower or more cumbersome. (General background knowledge.)

Practical mitigations and short-term validation strategies
- Increase and diversify retrieval corpora. Expand indexing to include multiple curated sources and representative domain literature; where feasible, augment the index with paraphrase-expanded passages to improve recall. Prioritize transparency about index composition so reviewers can interpret coverage limitations. (General background knowledge.)
- Retrieval re-ranking and ensemble methods. Apply secondary re-ranking models or heuristic filters (e.g., citation recency, venue signals, lexical overlap with queries) to reduce low-quality distractors exposed to the generator. Where available, use multiple retrieval algorithms and combine rankings to produce a consensus top-k. (General background knowledge.)
- Thresholding and conservative generation. Use strict thresholds on the amount and provenance of injected evidence required before permitting content that asserts factual claims; when evidence is insufficient, emit explicit uncertainty markers or leave placeholders for human authors to fill. (General background knowledge.)
- Human-in-the-loop verification. Integrate lightweight human checks at two points: (1) spot-check generated sections for unsupported assertions and (2) verify bibliographic integrity during assembly. Design the workflow so humans can correct JSON fields or swap evidence sources without re-running entire generations. (General background knowledge.)
- Robust JSON validation and graceful failure modes. Enforce schema validation as an early pipeline gate; on validation failure, return structured diagnostics (missing fields, type mismatches) and a reproducible regeneration request that includes the original evidence set and prompts. Keep logs of regeneration attempts for audit trails. (General background knowledge.)
- Automated unsupported-claim detectors and citation-coverage metrics. Employ conservative, high-precision heuristics to flag sentences that make factual claims lacking nearby evidence anchors; complement these with simple citation-coverage statistics (fraction of claims with an explicit source pointer) to prioritize human review. (General background knowledge.)
- Progressive deployment and ablations. Deploy the system in constrained, review-rich settings (e.g., internal drafts, closed-domain authoring) and run ablations that remove one component at a time (graph scheduling, evidence injection, JSON constraints) to isolate their effects before scaling to broader domains. (General background knowledge.)

Operational recommendations
- Track provenance and versioning. Record the evidence identifiers, prompt templates, and model checkpoints used to generate each section so that auditors can reproduce or re-run specific outputs. (General background knowledge.)
- Surface uncertainty to readers and reviewers. Where evidence is weak or absent, the system should generate explicit, machine-readable indicators of uncertainty or ``needs citation'' flags that downstream tooling and reviewers can act upon. (General background knowledge.)
- Prioritize tooling for editors. Invest in small UI features that let human editors accept, edit, or replace evidence citations in-place and revalidate JSON outputs; such tooling reduces friction and leverages human expertise efficiently. (General background knowledge.)

Concluding remark
All recommendations above are framed as conservative, practical mitigations intended to reduce unsupported assertions and improve auditability. Given the constrained evaluation resources noted in this paper, broader claims about the efficacy of individual mitigations should be validated in future work using larger, more diverse corpora and systematic ablation studies. (General background knowledge.)
